topic.title: 'DM for price' means it depends on you
topic.claim: 'DM for price' doesn't mean the price is complicated; it means the price depends on who's asking.
topic.moment: You like a kurta on Instagram, DM for the price, and wonder if they checked your profile first.

turn.believed: Sellers hide prices to keep the page clean or because prices change.
turn.actually: A private chat lets them read you first and quote what you look able to pay.

topic.feeling: I don't know if I was quoted fair or quoted my profile.
topic.villain: Private-chat selling with no listed price
topic.because: A public price is one price for everyone. A DM price can change with your city, your profile and how keen you sound.
topic.payoff: Test: ask from a friend's account too. If the two prices differ, you have your answer.
topic.behaviour: Small Instagram sellers hide prices and quote them in DMs.
topic.mechanism: No public price means room to charge each buyer differently.
topic.group: People who shop from small Instagram sellers
topic.send_to: The friend who buys everything from Instagram boutiques.
topic.why_now: Festive and wedding shopping on Instagram is at its peak.

score.why: 'DM for price' lets the seller read you before quoting, and the friend's-account test is easy to run.

sources.fact: The Competition Commission of India's 2022 cab-aggregator market study, as summarised by a law firm, found personalised pricing in controlled experiments, helped by rider data. It also said personalised pricing may not necessarily harm consumers. This is evidence from cab apps, not Instagram sellers.
sources.stance: neutral: It shows price personalisation using customer data is real in Indian markets. It says nothing about Instagram sellers, city, profile or how keen a buyer sounds. It also records that the aggregators denied rider attributes affect fares, and that no evidence of personalised pricing was found, so it only partly backs the claim.
sources.excerpt: Cab aggregators were perceived to be and found to be (based on the controlled real time experiments) engaging in personalised pricing. | the possession of personalised data on the consumers (i.e., riders) facilitated personalised pricing | There was no evidence to indicate that personalised pricing was practiced by the cab aggregators. | Personalised pricing may not necessarily lead to an adverse impact on consumer welfare

sources.fact: A marketing magazine says sellers hide prices mainly to get engagement and start private chats, not to charge different buyers different prices.
sources.stance: contradicts: It gives engagement and customer bonding as the reasons for 'DM for price'. It says nothing about quoting by city, profile or how keen the buyer sounds. This is opinion, not research.
sources.excerpt: What does a page want the most? The answer is engagement. | When prices are hidden, the first thing people will do is ask about it in the comments, so this increases the engagement. | it creates a bond between the customer and the brand.

cover.headline: 'DM for price' means the price depends on [who's asking]
cover.sub: Same kurta. A new price for every chat.

paragraphs: 'DM for price' doesn't mean the price is tricky. It means the price depends on who's asking.
slides.why_swipe: Who's asking? Surely it's the same kurta for everyone?

paragraphs: Every festive kurta set on a boutique page has the same line where the price should be. It says 'DM for price.'
So you DM. 'Typing…' starts and stops for a while.
Long enough to open your profile.
slides.why_swipe: Is that thought paranoid, or is something real going on?

paragraphs: Ask a seller why the price is hidden and you'll hear the usual reasons. A clean feed. Rates that keep changing. More people asking in the comments, which helps the post.
All fair. But a price tag can't see who's reading it. A chat can.

Before they type a number, they can see a lot:
– your city, from your bio
– the Goa trips and wedding outfits on your grid
– how badly you want it, because you wrote 'need it fast for a wedding'
slides.why_swipe: So what does all that change?

paragraphs: A price on the post has to work for everyone. In a chat, your number and the next person's number don't have to match.
Whatever extra you pay for looking like you can afford it, call it the profile tax.
Not every seller does. Most of these pages are one or two people, and plenty quote everyone the same.
The problem is the setup. A hidden price means you can't tell the honest seller from the one reading your grid.
slides.why_swipe: Then why do we keep buying this way?

paragraphs: We put up with it because the kurta is lovely. The seller feels like a person, not a company. Asking twice feels rude. Bargaining in someone's DMs feels worse.
slides.why_swipe: Is there a way to find out?

paragraphs: Try it once. Ask again from a friend's account, same kurta, same size.
If the numbers don't match, you just paid the profile tax.

end.save: Read it again before you DM a boutique for your next wedding outfit.
end.send: Send to the friend who buys every wedding outfit from Instagram boutiques and never asks twice.
end.promise: How selling in India really works.

draft.alt_text: A text-only Instagram carousel arguing that when small Instagram sellers write 'DM for price', a private chat lets them see your city, your profile and how keen you are before quoting, so your price and the next person's price don't have to match. It calls the extra you might pay for looking able to afford it the profile tax. It notes that many sellers quote everyone the same, but a hidden price means buyers can't tell which ones do. It ends with a test: ask for the same item from a friend's account and compare the two prices.
